title: The Statistical physics of unsaturated soil water: kinetic theory and non commutative pore water dynamics
abstract: We develop a statistical-mechanical theory of water in unsaturated soil whose outcome is a continuum field equation for the pore-occupancy g(r,x,t), the fraction of pores of radius r that are water-filled at position x and time t. The theory is built across three scales: microscopic inter-pore transfers set by Hagen-Poiseuille rates and a driving potential (the difference of pore-class chemical potentials, taken in capillary-gravitational form but open to adsorptive, osmotic, or thermal refinement); a mesoscale master equation relaxing the occupancy toward the equilibrium step g_eq=H(r*-r); and, on contracting the averaging volume to a point, the continuum balance d_t g + div F = C[g] - E - T, of which everything else is a limit, a moment, or a boundary resolution. The kinetic equation is an Onsager gradient flow descending the Gibbs free energy, with an H-theorem for the isothermal unforced system and mass conservation as its zeroth moment. A single dimensionless group, the pore-resolved Damkohler number Da(r,x), organizes the behavior and unifies phenomenologies long modelled separately. A Chapman-Enskog reduction identifies Richards' equation as the quasi-static (Da->0) limit, with matric potential and hydraulic conductivity K emerging only there and K vanishing below the percolation threshold; capillary-bundle and critical-path models are its diagonal and spectral limits. Hysteresis is the holonomy of a forcing bundle, a geometric phase rather than per-pore bistability, with a falsifiable loop-area law H ~ I^2. Preferential flow is what the same equation does where Da>1, so the Richards/preferential-flow dichotomy becomes a continuous Da-controlled crossover. Out of the quasi-static limit g(r) is the irreducible state variable. All inputs are geometric properties of the pore network, measurable from micro-CT and calibrated against no macroscopic data.
summary: This paper presents a unified statistical-mechanical theory for water transport in unsaturated soil. It derives a continuum field equation that naturally bridges the gap between slow, quasi-static flow (Richards' equation) and fast, non-equilibrium preferential flow regimes using a dimensionless Damköhler number. The work provides a rigorous framework based on minimizing free energy while accounting for rate-dependent memory effects.
main_problem: To develop a comprehensive statistical-mechanical theory for water dynamics in unsaturated soil that unifies classical rate-independent models with non-equilibrium, fast-flow regimes.
main_result:
The theory yields a continuum field equation ($\partial_t g + 
abla \cdot F = C[g] - E - T$) whose behavior is governed by the pore-resolved Damköhler number ($Da$), unifying quasi-static (Richards') and preferential flow regimes.
method: The theory constructs the dynamics across three scales—microscopic inter-pore transfers, mesoscopic master equations, and a continuum limit—identifying the evolution as an Onsager gradient flow descending the Gibbs free energy.
model_or_system: The system is unsaturated porous media (soil) characterized by pore radii ($r$) and position ($x$). The state variable is the pore-occupancy $g(r, x, t)$, which evolves based on chemical potential differences ($\Phi$) acting as the driving force.
key_observables: Pore-occupancy $g(r, x, t)$, hydraulic conductivity $K[g]$, hysteresis loop area ($H$), and the macroscopic water content $	heta$.
important_parameters: Pore-resolved Damköhler number $Da(r, x)$; capillary length ($\ell_c$); pore size distribution $f(r)$.
main_assumptions: Inputs (pore geometry) are assumed measurable from micro-CT; the theory is general and applies where local thermodynamic equilibria can be defined.
paper_structure: The paper builds the continuum equation by deriving it sequentially: first establishing microscopic transfer rates, then defining the mesoscopic master equation, and finally taking the continuum limit to obtain the full kinetic balance equation.
why_interesting: While focused on porous media, the framework of describing irreversible dynamics via an Onsager gradient flow descending a free energy functional is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics used in open quantum systems or complex chemical reaction networks.

FIG. 2. Flow partition under varying rainfall intensity on the 3 375-pore network. (a) Pore volume fraction in the matric (Da < 1, blue) and preferential (Da ≥1, red) regimes. (b) Flux fraction (r2-weighted): matric flux persists to higher I than matric volume because large, fast-equilibrating pores carry disproportionate flux. (c) Crossover radius rDa(I) ∝I0.59: the continuously shifting regime boundary. (d) Pore-size distribution with rDa boundaries at four representative intensities. At I = 5 mm/h, 71% of pore volume is already kinetic, but 84% of flux is still matric—explaining why Richards can appear adequate for water budgets when the pore-scale picture is far from equilibrium.
